messages.content: Return only JSON matching the supplied schema. Compare a full EVM smart-contract wallet operated by each sovereign enterprise against the following source-frozen requirements and technical facts. Authoritative legal facts: Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 applies from 2 August 2026. Providers of interactive AI systems must inform natural persons they are interacting with AI unless obvious. Providers of systems generating synthetic audio/image/video/text must machine-readably mark outputs and make them detectable, using solutions effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as technically feasible. Deployers must disclose emotion recognition/biometric categorisation, deepfakes, and AI-generated/manipulated public-interest text in the specified cases. Information must be clear, distinguishable, accessible and available by first interaction/exposure. The final June 2026 voluntary Code's provider section expects for most disseminable content two marking layers: digitally signed/time-stamped metadata and imperceptible watermarking; free-form text has special handling. It treats fingerprinting/logging as optional supplemental mechanisms, requires detection access, testing, monitoring, documentation, and accessibility, and permits third-party marking/detection providers without shifting ultimate provider responsibility. It requires watermark detection interoperability by 2 February 2027. Authoritative technical facts: an EVM smart-contract wallet can expose a stable address, validate arbitrary authorization logic and contract signatures, rotate/delegate signers according to its code, hold/pay tokens, and make on-chain transactions. A raw EVM address does not by itself bind to a legal person, embed metadata or watermarks into content, survive copy/paste or analogue transformations, create visible/accessibility disclosures, classify provider/deployer roles, or prove an asserted event happened. C2PA currently roots manifest trust in X.509 signing credentials and content binding rather than raw EVM addresses. Local settlement law makes each enterprise sovereign, requires explicit boundary contracts, treats x402 only as settlement of a real priced boundary, uses ActivityStreams/ActivityPub at enterprise borders and EAVT/Datom as monotone source log. Produce: contributions a wallet can make; requirements it cannot satisfy; architecture roles that must stay separate; and the strongest defensible formulation of the hypothesis. Do not recommend implementation or claim legal advice.

walletContributions: Stable EVM address provides a persistent, rotatable identity anchor that can be referenced in C2PA manifest metadata schemas to bind signing authority to a legal enterprise.

EIP-1271 contract signature validation enables the enterprise to delegate C2PA signing operations to third-party marking providers while retaining on-chain authorization control and ultimate responsibility.
Signer rotation and delegation logic creates an auditable on-chain record of who held marking authority at any point, supporting the documentation requirements of the Code.
On-chain transactions supply timestamped, immutable event entries usable as optional supplemental fingerprinting/logging records, satisfying the Code's supplemental (not primary) mechanism category.
Token holding and x402 payment settlement enables real-priced boundary transactions between sovereign enterprises, enforcing explicit boundary contracts at the ActivityPub federation layer.

Wallet-level delegation can formally designate third-party watermarking or detection service providers without shifting the enterprise's ultimate regulatory responsibility, consistent with the Code's allowance.
The stable address survives key compromise via signer rotation, allowing long-lived credential associations without invalidating historical provenance claims tied to the contract address.
unsatisfiedRequirements: The wallet cannot embed machine-readable C2PA manifests, XMP metadata, or signed provenance assertions directly into content files; content-binding requires a purpose-built marking pipeline.
Imperceptible perceptual watermarking of audio, image, video, and text outputs cannot be performed by a wallet; this requires dedicated signal-processing tooling in the content generation pipeline.
A raw EVM address does not survive copy-paste or analogue transformation; the Code requires marks that are robust and reliable across these transformations.
The wallet cannot generate the clear, distinguishable, accessible natural-person disclosure required at or before first interaction with an interactive AI system under Article 50.

Deployer-level disclosures for emotion recognition, biometric categorisation, deepfakes, and AI-generated public-interest text must appear at point of exposure; the wallet has no UX or presentation capability.
C2PA currently roots manifest trust in X.509 signing credentials, not raw EVM addresses; bridging EVM keys to C2PA trust anchors requires a separate PKI layer the wallet does not provide.
Watermark detection interoperability required by 2 February 2027 demands standardised detection APIs; the wallet exposes no detection surface.
The wallet cannot classify whether the enterprise is acting as provider or deployer for a given output, a distinction that determines which Article 50 obligations apply.
Free-form text outputs require special marking handling under the Code; the wallet has no mechanism to apply or enforce this treatment.

A blockchain transaction cannot prove that content was actually AI-generated or that a marking event occurred in the content pipeline; it proves only that a transaction was submitted claiming something.
Real-time monitoring, ongoing testing, and accessibility verification of marking systems required by the Code cannot be performed by or delegated to a wallet.
The wallet does not satisfy the requirement that information be available by first interaction/exposure, as it operates on-chain and is not visible to natural persons consuming content.
separateRoles: Identity/authorization anchor (wallet): holds stable address, rotates signers, validates EIP-1271 signatures — must remain separate from the content marking pipeline that actually embeds metadata and watermarks.
Content marking pipeline: embeds C2PA manifests, applies imperceptible watermarks, and performs X.509 signing — must not be conflated with the wallet's authorization layer.

Provider role vs. deployer role: Article 50 assigns distinct obligations to each; a single enterprise may occupy both, but the obligations cannot be discharged by a shared wallet without role-specific pipeline stages.

On-chain supplemental log (wallet transactions) vs. content-bound primary marks (C2PA/watermarks): the Code classifies these in separate mechanism tiers; treating the log as a primary mark is a category error.
PKI/X.509 credential layer: required by C2PA trust model; bridges EVM keys to recognised signing credentials and must be operated and audited separately from the wallet's key management.
Consumer-facing disclosure layer: natural-person notifications and accessibility requirements at point of interaction or exposure; entirely separate from enterprise-border settlement and federation.
ActivityStreams/ActivityPub federation boundary vs. C2PA content provenance: enterprise-border communication protocol conveys messages but does not embed or validate content marks.
EAVT/Datom monotone source log: authoritative internal provenance record for the enterprise; separate from and more authoritative than the supplemental on-chain transaction log.
Detection and interoperability service: the Code requires accessible detection APIs and third-party detection access; this is a distinct service role that must be independently operated and tested.
structured_output.defensibleHypothesis: An EVM smart-contract wallet can serve as a durable identity and authorization anchor — stable address, rotatable signing authority, third-party delegation, supplemental on-chain logging, and x402 settlement at enterprise boundaries — but it is neither a content-marking pipeline nor a disclosure surface. The strongest defensible claim: wallet infrastructure is necessary but radically insufficient for Article 50 and Code conformance, filling identity-anchor and settlement roles while leaving content-binding, watermarking, C2PA trust-chain rooting, natural-person disclosure, role classification, detection interoperability, and monitoring to purpose-built, separately governed pipeline stages.
structured_output.categoryErrorRisk: The primary category error is treating the wallet's stable address or on-chain transaction as a provenance assertion, watermark, or natural-person disclosure. A wallet address is an authorization anchor, not a content mark; conflating the two would produce an architecture that satisfies none of Article 50's output-marking or disclosure obligations while appearing to address them.
